speechtext:

Hawker Siddeley Canada Ltd. desperately requires orders, domestic or export, for its work force which forms the main industry for the town of Trenton, Nova Scotia. It is a key employer for the region. As I have had no substantive response from the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) in nearly three weeks to a request for assistance for this industry and for increased rail orders for Sydney Steel, I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Howie):
That in addition to financing projects like Algerian monuments through the Export Development Corporation, and preparing to undertake a $200 million Cl DA program for Trinidad and Tobago, to construct two airports and a prison, some comparable effort be made to assist industries like the ones I have mentioned which are terribly important to Canadians, on the basis that there is some substance to the saying that charity begins at home.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 rise pursuant to Standing Order 43. Equalization payments to poorer provinces so that Canadians, no matter where they live, all have reasonably comparable levels of public service, were thought to be so intrinsic to the nature of Canada that they are provided for in the new Constitution. The federal government must not compound its already tragic abandonment of cooperative federalism by adding to its attack on the funding for health care and post-secondary education the unilateral imposition of an equalization formula after only a short period of negotiations with the provinces. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans):
That the federal government withdraw its ultimatum to the provinces, restore funding for established programs financing to its full level, and look for an equalization formula that would more fully protect Canadians in have-not provinces from deterioration of public services.

subsubtopic: TRANSPORTATION OF DANGEROUS CHEMICALS IN MANITOBA- MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgency and importance to CN workers and residents in northern Manitoba. The material from a chemical spill at Austin, Manitoba, is being transported in open, uncovered cars by rail to Lynn Lake, Manitoba. These cars are stopped in transit on sidings within the town limits of the The Pas, Manitoba, raising concerns from the community about the danger of the chemicals to CN workers and people living in the vicinity.
Given the fact that workers were given no warning about the hazardous material they were handling-I wish the Conservatives cared about this-given the fact that the workers were given no warning about the hazardous material they were handling and were not wearing protective clothing, despite a previous telex from CN which promised that the chemicals would be covered and that protective gear would be provided to workers, 1 move, seconded by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Lewycky):
That there be an immediate investigation into this incident and into CN's overall procedures in the handling of dangerous chemicals, and further that the Minister of Labour stop stalling and immediately introduce amendments to Part IV of the Canada Labour Code which pertains to occupational health and safety.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister is aware that in May of 1981 cabinet passed a prerogative order with respect to peacetime and wartime emergency planning. This particular order involves a severe limitation of civil liberties. In fact, the cabinet order contains an extremely wide definition of "emergency" as determined by this cabinet.
Since this has never been debated by Parliament, I want to tell the Prime Minister that even the McDonald commission has strongly recommended that such emergency regulations be presented and tabled in Parliament and approved by Parliament prior to implementation.
I want to ask the Prime Minister under these circumstances, why was this particular order passed, particularly when there is no emergency legislation in place aside from implementation and invocation of the War Measures Act?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member refers to an order of May, 1981. I will have to refresh my memory on those parts of that order which the hon. member may find offensive. I do recollect that it was part of an exercise to update all emergency action which is provided for in case of floods, in case of any natural disasters, in case of insurrection or invasion. It covers the gamut.
The intention of the legislation is that there be a possibility in times of emergency, however defined, for Canadian authorities, including federal, provincial and municipal, to respond in a co-ordinated way. I am willing to take further questions indicating what particular aspect of the order the hon. member would find offensive and not consistent with the need for the
government to foresee co-ordinated action in terms of emergencies.

Madam Speaker, what is disconcerting is that the Prime Minister does not fully appreciate the fact that Parliament has not been seized with this particular matter. We have not had an opportunity to determine what the limitation of civil liberties will mean under this particular order, as well as its implications.
The Prime Minister has had a letter from the Joint Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments for over two months now and has not responded to some very pointed questions from the committee, representing all parties, forwarded in a letter signed by Senator Godfrey, the hon. member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore, and the member for Wellington-Dufferin-Simcoe.
The President of the Privy Council, when speaking to the joint federal-provincial conference on emergency planning, said last summer, as reported in the Emergency Planning Digest of July-September, 1981, that under certain circumstances if an emergency now took place the government would have no option but to act extra-legally, that is, outside the law. Is it now the policy of this government that the rule of law does not apply and should be ignored under certain circumstances of emergency in Canada?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext: No, Madam Speaker, under no circumstances should that be the case.
Madam Speaker, I would then suggest that the Prime Minister instruct the President of the Privy Council to have this matter rescinded and brought before Parliament before it is implemented.

The Prime Minister asked for an example in this particular order. The Prime Minister himself is mandated to manage and co-ordinate the national information services. Could the Prime Minister explain to the House what plans he has made, through his office, to manage and co-ordinate the so-called national information services? Could he also explain what is meant by the term "national information services"?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext: No, Madam Speaker, I know of no such plans. I would imagine that in order to answer the question one would have to refer to the type of action which was taken by the Canadian government- I believe with the support of all parties in the House-during the Second World War-

This is peacetime.
February 24, 1982
-to exercise certain measures of censorship and so forth. That was during the war. 1 imagine this kind of monitoring of information would be necessary again in the event of a third world war.
In peacetime?

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Solicitor General. Under this cabinet order respecting emergencies in both peacetime and wartime, is the Solicitor General in charge of the establishment and operation of civilian internment camps and, if so, where are they, how many are there, and who will be subject to internment?
Apart from us.

Madam Speaker, it has often been alleged that during World War II Canada was very unjust to minority groups, and particularly to Japanese Canadians, in the way these groups were treated. One of the reasons was that no planning had been done in advance to prepare our country and to prepare the government to deal with an invasion or the possibility of an invasion, war, or other major catastrophies in the event of which Canadians could rightly look to their government to be prepared to deal with emergencies.
Who is next?

I can confirm to the hon. member that I have been asked-and the order has been made public-to begin planning for the eventuality he described, but I have not yet begun to look at any plans, and I am not yet in a position to give any concrete details because none have yet been developed, beyond regulations which were created many years ago and which are sitting on the shelf and available for any member of the public to see.

Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the Prime Minister. Because there are no safeguards of any type relating to civil or political rights in this cabinet order, which is broad enough to cover both peacetime problems as well as wartime problems-and certainly there are no safeguards inserted in the antiquated and sole piece of legislation we have, and there have been none inserted in the War Measures Act since the FLQ crisis 11 years ago-why has new emergency legislation not been brought forward to this House as promised by the Prime Minister many times before now, and when will we see that new legislation?

subtopic: CUTBACK IN PRODUCTION OF HEAVY CRUDE OIL
CUTBACK IN PRODUCTION OF HEAVY CRUDE OIL
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and concerns the plight of Canadian heavy oil producers. As the minister knows, at least partly due to the import compensation program, refiners in Montreal are using subsidized imported heavy crude oil, while Canadian producers of heavy crude are severely cut back. The result is an unneeded extra cost to consumers, an unneeded extra current account drain, and an unneeded loss of income and thus of jobs to Canadian producers. What is the minister doing about this situation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: CUTBACK IN PRODUCTION OF HEAVY CRUDE OIL
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there are indeed circumstances where, because of a drop in the price of oil on the international market and especially on-the-spot market, refiners are able to obtain certain products, on a short-term basis, at prices that are lower than they would be paying if they were buying Canadian crude oil. Such cases are, however, very limited in number. We are following developments very closely.
I may also point out to the hon. member that in several cases, as a result of the cuts imposed by Alberta last year, companies have had to conclude medium and long-term contracts. They are very hesitant to break these contracts now, considering the present situation. More specifically, they are
Oral Questions
afraid they will be needing foreign oil in a few months, and they want to avoid jeopardizing trade relations with the parties with whom they signed contracts in good faith. It is a matter of concern, we are looking into it, and if any action should be taken, I shall be informing the House accordingly.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I rise on a particularly timely point of privilege which relates to the Metric Commission-

subsubtopic: MR. DOMM-ALLEGED CONTEMPTUOUS COMMENTS MADE BY PUBLIC SERVANT
speechtext:
-and my ability as an elected member of this Parliament to fulfil and properly discharge my duties. I will show Your Honour how, in fact, this ability as a Member of Parliament has been seriously impaired by my having been referred to contemptuously and in an insulting manner by one in the employ of the Public Service of Canada. What is more, these remarks were not made by that person privately, not made by him as a citizen, but made in a professional capacity
Privilege-Mr. Domm
on behalf of his employer, the Metric Commission of Canada, and directly to a representative of the press.
No one more than 1 values and cherishes the right of every citizen freely to criticize the government in any one of its varied and broad aspects and programs. Indeed, 1 could not agree more with the judgment of a former speaker of the House of Commons who, when speaking to a similar question of privilege on June 23, 1977, as reported at page 7044 of Hansard, noted, in citing a study by a committee of the U.K. parliament, that:
-Ihc House should be slow and reluctant to use its penal powers to stifle criticism or even abuse, whether of the machinery of the House, of a member or of an identifiable group of members, however strongly the criticism may be expressed and however unjustifiable it may appear.
Your committee regard such criticism as the lifeblood of democracy. In their view, the sensible politician expects and even welcomes criticism of this nature.
I entirely endorse this view and gladly subscribe to it. My purpose is not to complain about some private or even corporate remark made by an individual on behalf of himself, his firm, or his organization which impugns my reputation and which happens by accident or design to be picked up and reported in the press. On the contrary, this I would consider to be fair game and part of political life, which must be taken along with the more favourable reports of one's efforts here in the House of Commons, in one's riding, and in the country generally.
My purpose is to bring to the attention of the Chair and of the House of Commons a situation which is quite outside the normal purview of democratic licence and of the constitutional exercise of freedom of speech soon to be adopted. It concerns the on the record, gratuitous and deliberate abuse of an incumbent Member of Parliament by one who is in the employ of, and speaks for, an agency or department of government.
We know what happens when a public servant presumes to recognize his ancient mandate within our democratic tradition by criticizing the government non-abusively, without rancour, and on matters totally beyond his area and field of employment. He is fired with little fanfare and less ceremony, ruthlessly, deliberately, and without hesitation or the least application of enlightened principle. Mr. Neil Fraser of Revenue Canada in Kingston, Ontario, a senior official with 11 years experience and a salary range in excess of $40,000 a year, recently suffered this gross indignity. But we do not know what happens when an individual employed by the federal government to further an official program of that government and speaking in this professional capacity presumes not just to criticize the point of view, but also the attitudes and actions of a sitting Member of Parliament, actions which the member considers to be dutiful and in keeping with his place in the Government of Canada, for indeed the House is where the Government of Canada ultimately resides.
Now while 1 can fully support the opinion of the U.K. committee as cited by the previous speaker in 1977, I would

February 24, 1982
Privilege-Mr. Domm
now draw Your Honour's attention to a further remark from the same source and likewise cited:
Nevertheless, a point may be reached at which conduct ceases to be merely intemperate criticism and abuse and becomes or is liable to become an improper obstruction of the functions of Parliament. For such cases, however rare, the penal powers must be preserved and the House must be prepared to exercise them.
On November 25, 1981, an individual employed by the Metric Commission, a Mr. Bob Mellor, was interviewed by Ms. Judy Creighton, a reporter for the Canadian Press. Subsequently, Ms. Creighton's report went out nationally, and in it Mr. Mellor is directly quoted as having referred to me as "the anti-metric red-neck from Peterborough".

subsubtopic: MR. DOMM-ALLEGED CONTEMPTUOUS COMMENTS MADE BY PUBLIC SERVANT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, with your indulgence, 1 will first put this remark in a general context according to the standard references, and then in a more specific context which reflects a more contemporary point of view. Both, I believe, are germane.
First, the House will know of the guidance offered by Erskine May at Chapter X, pages 152 and 153 where it is noted that:
'Written imputations, as affecting a Member of Parliament, may amount to breach of privilege, without perhaps, being libels at common law' (b), but to constitute a breach of privilege a libel upon a member must concern the character or conduct of the member in that capacity (c).
Continuing on to page 153, it is stated that:
Both Houses will punish not only contempts arising out of facts of which the ordinary courts will take cognizance, but those of which they cannot, such as contemptuous insults, gross calumny or foul epithets by word of mouth not within the category of actionable slander or threat of bodily injury.
Going on, I submit that in the first instance my question of privilege fulfils these terms. If you see fit, I would suggest the following motion, which I have submitted to you, under Standing Order 17, which was found to be acceptable as reported at page 7044 of Hansard for June 23, 1977, at which time the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland (Mr. Lawrence) presented a number of motions and they were accepted to be in order:
That this House do recognize that contemptuous insults have been directed toward me by officials of the government and as reported in the national press, that these contemptuous insults reflect upon my conduct as a Member of Parliament, and that the full penal jurisdiction of this House of Commons be applied to the extent that this high violation of the rights and privileges of the House are repaired.
I use as my authority for that language in the motion Erskine May, page 152 and part of page 153. Some members may not consider that term "red-neck" particularly contemptuous or insulting. For their information, I refer to the Oxford American dictionary which at the entry for "red-neck" has in parenthesis the word "contemptuous". That is the key to my question of privilege. The definition follows as "a member of the white, rural working class of the southern United States". That is hardly an accurate description of me and, needless to say, one which I strongly resent.
The more specific context within which these remarks fall deals with the citizen's prima facie right to make a fair comment "upon such activity of a member as a matter of public interest." As the committee said, and as was repeated by the then Speaker in 1977, "His right is even stronger to speak and publish the truth of a member's conduct".
We know, as I have said, what will happen to a citizen who speaks against the conduct of members for Mount Royal (Mr. Trudeau) and Papineau (Mr. Ouellet). The former heads the present government; the latter is responsible for the Metric Commission. When Mr. Neil Fraser of Kingston questioned their conduct with regard to the metrication of Canada, he was fired. The famous and justly faceless official of Revenue Canada answered for his political leaders in the press by saying "It is a standard condition of federal government employment that an employee may not make any public criticism of government policy or its political leaders."
Does this not seem to contradict the judgment of the parliamentary committee and of the Speaker of the House who said in 1977 that "these rights of free speech should not in the normal way be defeated'? Does it not contradict the Speaker's judgment that criticism is the "lifeblood of democracy"? Does it not contradict the Speaker's judgment that "as elected people", for we are all elected people, even the members for Mount Royal and Papineau, "we can and do expect to be the targets of attack'? At any rate, Mr. Fraser's lamentable case applies to my question of privilege by illuminating through comparison.
The person who criticized me, or rather was responsible for directing a contemptuous insult toward me, to use May's phrase, was not speaking as a private citizen. He spoke as an employee of the government. We have seen what has happened to another employee of the government who levelled what in comparison must be seen to be the gentlest criticism at the government.
How will my grievance be redressed as a member of this government in opposition-for surely Parliament, all of Parliament, is an integral part of the Government of Canada- as a consequence of my being not only criticized, but abused by this gross and contemptuous insult? I ask then that my question be taken under advisement with a view toward applying the statutory penal jurisdiction of the House of Commons.
Before placing the motion, I would like to add some brief comments. I am now going to show the House that the acting executive director of the Metric Commission needs to be immediately fired from his job, the same as Mr. Neil Fraser was fired.
Mr. Ganapathy, the acting executive director of the Metric Commission, referred to me in a contemptuous and insulting manner on the CBC program "Platform". Everyone knows that the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, with the blessing of the Metric Commission, forced retail grocers out of business when they refused to use metric weigh scales in Peterborough.
February 24, 1982

I regret to inform the House that Mr. Ganapathy went on the CBC program "Platform" and refuted this statement, and he did not just refute this statement made by me as a Member of Parliament in opposition, but said, "That is a lot of nonsense what the member for Peterborough is saying, and that is not true."
How can a responsible civil servant get away with calling a Member of Parliament, a member of the opposition, a liar and hold his job when at the same time Mr. Neil Fraser, who said, "The white paper of 1970 on metric conversion was to bring metric in voluntarily and the government has now decided to break its promise and bring it in by force," loses his job, and yet Mr. Ganapathy who calls me a liar, a gentleman who has never been to Peterborough, as he admitted over national television, does not know the merchants 1 am talking about, knows better than 1 do as the Member of Parliament for Peterborough that my businesses were forced out of business because they would not buy a metric weigh scale? As acting executive director of the Metric Commission, he must be fired.
Second, I think I have already shown that we have allowed two categories of MPs to be created in the House. Knowingly or not, our present government, the members sitting opposite, have created a situation where a civil servant is allowed to make contemptuous, insulting statements against a Member of Parliament, provided that member is a member of the opposition and not on the government side of the House.
I am going to name that civil servant, which 1 have already done, and I will name him again, because that civil servant should no longer be on the payroll of the Government of Canada and going around this country telling people that Members of Parliament in opposition are red-necks. If he does not know what the word means, somebody should tell him. If he does know what it means, he has no business being in the job he is, criticizing a Member of Parliament in a contemptuous way, according to the Oxford dictionary, which is the best authority I can find on the term "red-neck".
Having named that civil servant, Mr. Ganapathy, the acting executive director of the Metric Commission for Canada, is not better. How can the House of Commons condone a situation whereby it allows willingly that any civil servant who criticizes the government in power is out of a job and any civil servant who criticizes the opposition maintains a secure job because he is doing the job for the government, not for the people? I maintain that is not right. Therefore I move, under Standing Order 17:
That this House do recognize that contemptuous insults have been directed toward me by officials of the government and as reported in the national press and on the CBC program "Platform", that these contemptuous insults reflect upon my conduct as a Member of Parliament and that the full penal jurisdiction of this House of Commons be applied to the extent that this high violation of the rights and privileges of the House are immediately repaired.
With all due respect, Madam Speaker, this matter should be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections for a full parliamentary investigation into who civil servants represent. Do they work for the government or do they work for the Parliament of Canada and the people? I maintain that it is time civil servants were allowed to speak out
Privilege-Mr. Domm
of their jurisdiction in the private sector, before municipal councils as ratepayers in those communities on behalf of their rights when they have invested in property in their communities. Since they have the right to vote municipally, they certainly must have the right to say what they think about matters that they are not even directly connected with in the government's business of the day. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

subsubtopic: MR. DOMM-ALLEGED CONTEMPTUOUS COMMENTS MADE BY PUBLIC SERVANT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. David Smith (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: MR. DOMM-ALLEGED CONTEMPTUOUS COMMENTS MADE BY PUBLIC SERVANT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have listened with considerable interest to the alleged question of privilege raised by the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm) in trying to figure out what it was. I have not yet figured it out.
It seems to me that his proposition was based somehow on a statement which he made, and I found it difficult to believe. I believe he made the statement, and it can be verified on the record, of course. He said that Parliament was a part of the Government of Canada. Of course, Parliament is not a part of the Government of Canada.

subsubtopic: MR. DOMM-ALLEGED CONTEMPTUOUS COMMENTS MADE BY PUBLIC SERVANT
speechtext: You are right.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: MR. DOMM-ALLEGED CONTEMPTUOUS COMMENTS MADE BY PUBLIC SERVANT
speechtext:
An employee of Parliament is very different from an employee of the Government of Canada. If my hon. friend from Peterborough does not yet understand that, I suggest that he go to the library and obtain a first-year text on political science in Canada.
I believe that we are basically talking about a statement made by an employee of the Government of Canada. If you refer to Beauchesne, fifth edition, at page 12, section 19(1), it says:
A dispute arising between two members, as to allegations of facts, does not fulfil the conditions of parliamentary privilege.
It seems to me even clearer that a dispute arising between a Member of Parliament and a citizen as to an allegation of fact is even less a question of privilege. Surely that is the situation which exists here.
I do not believe that the hon. member for Peterborough suggested that this particular civil servant called him a liar or any such name. There seems to be a dispute as to facts. There seems to be a dispute as to the question of fact, and that does not, Madam Speaker, in any way raise a question of privilege, to my understanding.
The hon. member also quoted from Erskine May. I have read those quotations. It says at page 152, " .. . but to constitute a breach of privilege, a libel upon a member must concern the character or conduct of the member in that capacity." I do not recall hearing anything which constituted anything other than a dispute as to facts, not something which was an imputation concerning the character or conduct of the member. Therefore, I would suggest that what we are dealing with here is a dispute as to facts between a member of the House and a

February 24, 1982
Privilege-Mr. Domm
private citizen, and that certainly does not raise a question of privilege in the House.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. DOMM-ALLEGED CONTEMPTUOUS COMMENTS MADE BY PUBLIC SERVANT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I will be brief. The hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm) raises a very interesting and rare question of privilege which is deserving of very careful consideration by you.
I was surprised to hear the interjection by the parliamentary secretary. I had occasion to study this matter very carefully a few months ago when remarks which I felt at the time to be extremely contemptuous, were made in the French press in Quebec where a list of names of all the Liberal Members of Parliament appeared and, if I remember correctly, I believe they were described as despicable traitors. I fully expected that one or more of those members would have raised a question of privilege at that time based precisely on the argument made by the hon. member for Peterborough today. I do not think there is a member of the House who would not have been sympathetic to such a question had it been raised. However, that was the purpose of my studying the matter a few months ago.
This relates very directly to the question raised by the hon. member for Peterborough under several references to Erskine May as to what amounts to contempt. I submit that the hon. member for Peterborough does have a good case. The words which were used were contemptuous of the conduct of the hon. member in his capacity as a Member of Parliament and member of the House of Commons.
1 am sure that the Chair is aware of the rarity of questions of this nature being raised in this place. I fear that perhaps the Chair might come to the conclusion that it should not be called upon to make a decision as to whether or not the offender should continue his employment because of one of the remarks made by the hon. member for Peterborough. 1 suggest that the Chair would be perfectly correct in coming to the conclusion that it has no business interfering in that area. However, the remedy which seemed to emerge from my studies of the question when I was considering whether or not the remarks of the French press against the Liberal members concerned would be contemptuous, was that the proper recourse-and certainly the power exists in the Chair acting on behalf of all members of the House-was to have the offender appear before the bar of the House.
1 believe the last time that happened was so long ago that the official record of the House of Commons, Hansard, was not even an established institution of this place but was still being published in local newspapers. I had to go back to those newspapers to dig out the precedents. However, the precedents are there, and I think that the offender in that case was from the city of Winnipeg.
The House, then, has the power indeed to go as far as to impose a jail term on an offender unless other solutions are
found.
1 would suggest that there is a serious substance to the question which has been placed before you. It is sufficiently serious, I submit, to cause you to defer your decision on the
matter until a study of this very rare procedure might be made by the Chair and its assistants in some depth.
Once again, I can only relate back to those rather shoddy newspaper advertisements which I noticed when I was studying the matter and say that had the question been raised by one or more of the Liberal members at that time, they would have found support from this side of the House for their position alleging contempt for their rights as members. I ask for that same support from that side now when the same contemptuous remarks have been made with respect to the conduct of a member on this side of the House while carrying out his duties as a Member of Parliament.
A person employed by the government has no right to make public criticisms of a contemptuous nature. That distinction must be drawn. What the hon. member for Peterborough said about the right of free speech is absolutely correct, but there are limits on anyone's free speech. That is the reason for the law of libel and slander in this and any other civilized country. Those limits were exceeded in the remarks made by this government employee when he referred to the hon. member for Peterborough as a red-neck, particularly knowing that the hon. member has specialized in being the chief critic for our party of forced metrication.
I do urge that you defer your decision, Madam Speaker, and study the matter. It will be my submission that you find in favour of the member for Peterborough, and either exercise the always undisturbed jurisdiction of the House and have the offender appear before the bar of the House or perhaps, as the hon. member for Peterborough suggested, refer the subject matter of his question to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.

subsubtopic: MR. DOMM-ALLEGED CONTEMPTUOUS COMMENTS MADE BY PUBLIC SERVANT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I do not know how you will ever rule on a matter such as this. The hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm) makes an interesting case about being offended by the remarks of a public servant. I hope, however-and I say this in all fairness-that we in the House would never attempt to invoke privilege to prevent any citizen from commenting on the appropriateness or inappropriateness of anything we as Members of Parliament might say.
1 think it unfortunate that the hon. member tied his comments to the most recent firing which has taken place over comments made by an employee of the Department of National Revenue inasmuch as I hoped, as I listened to his argument, he would agree with me that the firing of the gentleman from the Department of National Revenue was inappropriate and that that particular gentleman form the Department of National Revenue, who is now in the process of appealing his dismissal, will have his appeal upheld. The right of every single citizen in Canada to express his or her opinion about the actions not only of the government but also of Parliament as a whole and individual Members of Parliament should in no way be impeded by an action taken by the House.
February 24, 1982

1 can appreciate that the hon. member for Peterborough believes in good faith that he was perhaps maligned in one way or another and that the person making the comments about the truthfulness or otherwise of the statements of the hon. member for Peterborough may have spoken out of turn. It may well be that in the normal relationship between citizens and their elected members this particular citizen stated his point of view a little more forcefully than might have been required in the circumstance. However, I put it to the Chair that there are many things said in the House of Commons which are much worse than calling a member of the Conservative Party a redneck. In fact, for some that might even be a compliment.
I therefore hope that in viewing this matter Your Honour will find that we ought not to interfere with the rights of citizens to express their opinions, no matter for whom they work and no matter in what ministry they are employed.

subsubtopic: MR. DOMM-ALLEGED CONTEMPTUOUS COMMENTS MADE BY PUBLIC SERVANT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I want briefly to supplement the remarks of my House leader and say that it was with considerable astonishment that I heard the remarks-and I listened with great care-of the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm). His party was championing the right of freedom of speech only an hour earlier on behalf of public servants and was bitterly decrying-in my view quite properly-the firing of Neil Fraser in Kingston because Mr. Fraser was speaking on a matter of public policy.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. DOMM-ALLEGED CONTEMPTUOUS COMMENTS MADE BY PUBLIC SERVANT
speechtext: Not contemptuously.

subsubtopic: MR. DOMM-ALLEGED CONTEMPTUOUS COMMENTS MADE BY PUBLIC SERVANT
speechtext: Following this attack, an attack with which this party agrees, what did a member of the Conservative Party do? He stood up and suggested that because he has been attacked as being a red-neck-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. DOMM-ALLEGED CONTEMPTUOUS COMMENTS MADE BY PUBLIC SERVANT
speechtext: Libeled.

subsubtopic: MR. DOMM-ALLEGED CONTEMPTUOUS COMMENTS MADE BY PUBLIC SERVANT
speechtext:
-what we should do is to haul this public servant before the bar of Parliament and perhaps throw him in jail. What unbridled hypocrisy on the part of the Conservative Party in this Parliament! What unbridled hypocrisy!
Members of the Conservative Party proclaim the right to freedom of speech on behalf of all Canadians, but if they themselves are attacked in their role as Members of Parliament, do they allow that freedom of speech? No. What they suggest under those circumstances is that we bring that person before Parliament and perhaps throw him in jail because we cannot legally take his job away. Members of the Conservative party speak on the one hand of freedom of speech for public servants, if those public servants happen to espouse the policies they believe in, but if those public servants happen to criticize the policies they support, then it is a very different story, and they take great offence.
Well, Madam Speaker, we do not accept that. We support the right of Neil Fraser to speak out on matters of public policy, and we insist upon his rehiring, if freedom of speech in
Privilege-Mr. Domm
this country is to mean anything and if the right accorded under the Charter of Rights and Freedoms to freedom of speech is to mean anything.
However, we go further and say that we as Members of Parliament should not be immune to that kind of criticism. To suggest that because we are criticized, whether rightly or wrongly-and I make no comment on the colour of the hon. member's neck-for the job we do or the policies we espouse, somehow that individual should be brought before Parliament and thrown in some sort of medieval parliamentary jail is utter hypocrisy, and I call upon the Chair to reject it, and to reject it now.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. DOMM-ALLEGED CONTEMPTUOUS COMMENTS MADE BY PUBLIC SERVANT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 hope in your ruling you will stick to the point at issue, which is whether a federal civil servant has the right to make derogatory and libellous remarks about a Member of Parliament. If the hon. member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) felt so strongly about freedom of speech, where were he and his party during question period? We heard not a peep from them during question period about freedom of speech for federal civil servants. We heard not a thing.
I ask you, Madam Speaker, to ignore the remarks of the hon. member for Burnaby, to look at this issue and not to pay any attention to the cheap political rhetoric of the hon. member for Burnaby.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. DOMM-ALLEGED CONTEMPTUOUS COMMENTS MADE BY PUBLIC SERVANT
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm) for submitting this question of privilege. He gave me proper notice, and he has quoted the relevant citation from Erskine May, which I would like to consider at length against the arguments and facts he has brought forward.
I am just a little wary about the fact that this incident took place, I believe, on November 25, 1981. When questions of privilege are raised in the House, every other proceeding must be stopped, the implication being that if they are not dealt with immediately the proceedings of the House may not continue. However, I will take this question of privilege under advisement.

subsubtopic: MR. DOMM-ALLEGED CONTEMPTUOUS COMMENTS MADE BY PUBLIC SERVANT

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 rise to speak on second reading of this legislation. Today notice has been given of a motion to impose closure on debate. I do not know why hon. members opposite want to impose closure
Housing
on a piece of legislation which is such a feeble effort to overcome the housing crisis in the country.
First of all 1 should like to speak about the need for housing in Canada today-
Speak about your trip.

1 will deal with my last trip when I come to it but 1 am not going to the great roundup for a while yet!
I want to deal first with the need that exists, and then with how these needs were viewed by the Liberal party several years ago. 1 will go on to deal with the solutions that the governmet proposes and their inadequacy. After that I will outline what we proposed and point out how the people of Canada would have been helped had we not been stopped by the NDP-Liberal conspiracy to restrain justice in Canada in December, 1979. 1 will then go on to make some suggestions about what should be done to help the people of Canada.
First of all, we must ask ourselves what some of the needs for action are in the housing field today. We only have to consult the latest CMHC report to see what the need is. A report published yesterday by the Canadian Press reads in part as follows:
High interest rates will cause housing starts to fall by 9 per cent and will make 1982 another bad year for the housing industry-
Referring of CMHC, the second paragraph reads as follows:
The federal Crown corporation predicts little change in mortgage rates during the first half of this year and perhaps slightly higher rates in the second half.
Mortgage rates are now running at about 19 per cent, Mr. Speaker, and the government's own agency, Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, expects the rates to be higher in the second half of the year. The article states that housing starts are expected to drop to about 162,000 units this year compared to 177,973 units last year.
1 might point out that in 1976, the best year the country has had for housing starts, 273,203 units were built. This year it is expected that 100,000 fewer will be constructed. Has the population of Canada somehow declined or vanished if we need 100,000 fewer housing starts this year than in 1976? Of course it has not.
The article goes on to say that corporation predicts that this year starts on single-detached houses will drop to 83,000. Imagine, Mr. Speaker, in this whole gigantic country from St. John's, Newfoundland, to Vancouver Island, there will be
83,000	starts on single detached homes in 1982. This is the marvellous record of the hon. gentlemen opposite who have been in office for two years and whose record is so shameful that one would expect them to leave quietly without even calling an election. They should vanish from the country in shame at such a record.
CMHC forecast that for my own province of Newfoundland there will be 3,500 housing starts this year, Madam Speaker.

February 24, 1982
Housing
That is a pitiful number. In the highest and best year for housing starts, over 5,000 were built in that province. I do not have the figures in front of me but as I recollect, the figure is 3,500 as compared to 2,000 more in 1978, which was the year with the highest number of starts in Newfoundland.
For evidence of just how bad the situation is I refer to a report which appeared in The Globe and Mail on May 27, 1981. It quotes Mr. Richard Shiff, Chairman of Bramalea Ltd. of Brampton as follows:
What we are witnessing is a financial crisis that has squeezed low and middle-income families out of the market.
He says it will squeeze them out of the market. Well, Mr. Speaker, he should know; that is his company's business. The article goes on to say:
He estimated that an Ontario family would have to have a combined income of $46,000 this year to afford a $70,000 mortgage, representing a 40 per cent cost increase in the past year.
He said:
Less than 10 per cent of Canadian families, who are currently renting, earn this level of income.
In other words, less than 10 per cent of Canadian families can expect today ever to own their own homes or ever to have the opportunity of owning their own homes. Of course he ascribed a great deal of blame to government housing policies and to the high interest rate situation of today, which he said has reached the outrageous height of 19.5 per cent. One of his recommendations was to permit home owners to deduct from income for tax purposes mortgage interest expenses above a realistic mortgage rate of about 13 per cent. He estimated that it would cost the government about $500 million in 1981 alone.
This reminds me of the solution we put forward in the House in December 1979 which was defeated-and I will come to that in more detail in a few minutes-by a combination of the Liberal Party and the New Democratic Party, which cared not a whit about helping home owners of Canada or those who might want to become home owners when they have that opportunity.
What other evidence about the need for action in housing do we require? I am looking now at a column by Dian Cohen which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen on November 3. Her calculation was that from 85,000 to 100,000 people could lose their homes in Canada in the next year. She quoted Mr. Claude Renaud, vice-president of the Mortgage Insurance Company of Canada, who estimated that 70,000 home owners will have nothing to fall back on when they renegotiate their loans as they come due during the present year. There we have
70,000	to 100,000 home owners with mortgages who, as Dian Cohen, the economist, and Mr. Renaud, vice-president of the Mortgage Insurance Company of Canada, say, will not be able to renegotiate their mortgage renewals this year and will lose their homes. Somebody on the opposite side might start croaking, "What evidence do you have that anybody is losing his or her home?"
Just in my district of St. John's West, Newfoundland, I have more than sufficient evidence. I should like to refer to a letter that was sent to me just this week. It is a letter from Judith Murphy of 228 Mundy Pond Road in St. John's West. Mrs. Murphy herself is in dire straits, as the government likes to call it. She wrote a letter to the newspaper on September 12, 1981. She sent a copy of the letter she had written to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in which she pointed out how, after being married 11 years, her husband and she now have to do battle with double mortgage payments. Three years ago they managed to purchase a new home of their own. Now they are faced with the prospect of losing it because of high interest rates. She asked the Pime Minister to do something about it, to help her keep her home so that her two children will have the benefit of growing up in their own home and not in tenement housing. In the letter she said:
There are no words to describe to you how it feels to be on the threshold of losing the security which one dreams of having in being a home owner.
I must confess to you that there is possibly one way to hold on to my home, that is if we really cut back, and what I mean by cutting back, more so than I already have, is to stop buying food.
She has nothing left to cut back on. She continued:
I have two children, they don't get to travel to faraway places on vacation, they enjoy the back garden.
They do not go to Morocco, they do not go to Kenya, and they do not go on summer vacations to North Africa with papa because papa does not have the Government of Canada and its huge exchequer behind him to send him and his children to these exotic countries of the world. No, this woman has only her own backyard for those two children to travel to during the summer, so she realizes that the Prime Minister will not understand how it feels to her. She said:
We can't afford a vacation-
This is not a crank letter-I am sure I have voiced the thoughts of thousands more like me.
She wanted a reply from the Prime Minister by return mail as to what he could do. Of course she did not receive any reply from the Prime Minister as to what she could do, but she received a reply from me as to what she could do. I told her that there was very little she could do as long as the government was in power-this government which does not care, this government which will deceive and use deceit to get into power and then will just forget every promise or obligation it made during the few months it was out of power.
Also, Mrs. Judith Murphy sent me the advertisements in the St. John's newspaper of foreclosures and forced sales of houses under mortgages in just one week. In my district of St. John's West, there were 17 sales under mortgages in that particular week which she clipped from the paper. These are the notices of sales under the power of sale, all in my district. With the exception of one sale in Chamberlain and one sale in Gander, the other 15 are from St. John's West. All of those homes were held under mortgages. Here is one on 81 Munden Drive, Mount Pearl, it was sold on Monday, February 22. This is a person in dire straits who had his home sold just on Monday. If anyone is looking for bargains, I can give them other addresses in Mount Pearl and throughout St. John's West-Ferryland,
February 24, 1982

St. Vincent's and Colinet in my district. These houses all went up for sale under powers of sale this month. This shows the need. The government should not tell us that there is no need.
Also, I have a petition from Mrs. Murphy with 38 names of people who are in dire straits or in this perilous situation themselves. Now, if a person has a $30,000 mortgage and has to pay 19 per cent interest on it this year, it will cost $5,700 in interest alone. A $30,000 mortgage is not a large mortgage. The average small three-bedroom home in Newfoundland today costs at least $60,000. A piece of land in St. John's, now serviced to build on, costs $30,000. One cannot get it for under $30,000, but a $30,000 mortgage at 19 per cent costs $5,700 per year.
What about Mrs. Murphy? On February 9 she wrote that her husband's gross salary in 1981 was $15,600 and that her gross salary was $9,000. These are not lazy people, they have two children and they are both working. She wrote:
How would Mr. Trudeau like to feed and clothe and house his children on that?
He has been cuddled into the bosom of government for years, since 1968, paying for nothing. He has been over at 24 Sussex Drive and at Harrington Lake. He does not have to worry about salaries of $15,600 or $9,000. He has a staff to look after his children, nannies, nursemaids, and everything under the sun, but Mrs. Murphy has to. She said that they got into their home three years ago under the assisted home ownership program at a lower interest rate. Now she faces a renewal, and God knows what she will have to renew her mortgage at. If it is at a 19 per cent interest rate or anything over 12 per cent or 13 per cent, they are finished; they will lose their home.
What else is evident in these? 1 have another clipping from the Montreal Gazette on January 26, 1982 which reads:
There were almost three million Canadians living in poverty in 1980, about 200,000 more than in 1979-
After all the promises and protestations of the "marvellous" Prime Minister which the country has had since 1968 about the just society, we see three million Canadians were living in poverty in 1980, which was 200,000 more than the year before. The article continued:
-639,000 families and 826,000 single people were poor in 1980-
That is 10.4 per cent of all families and 31.4 per cent of all singles in Canada in 1980-
This was a study carried out by the National Council of Welfare. There can be no doubt of the need for relief of home owners from high interest rates. 1 will come to what they are offered in this legislation in a few minutes.
By the way, the starts in Newfoundland in 1976 were 5,709. In 1978 they went down to 2,865. In 1981 they were 3,210, down 2,492 from the peak year of 1976. This year they estimate that it will be 3,500. What are the interest rates today compared with a year or so ago? Wait until 1 find my note; if I am unable to do so, I will give the interest rates from memory.
Housing
That will never do.

I have a fantastic memory, so I will do it from memory. The interest rates in December 1979 and in March 1980 when the government took over were 14 per cent at the Bank of Canada; that was the bank rate. Mortgage rates were down around 12 per cent or 13 per cent. The interest rates at the bank, at the highest, had gone to 15 per cent when we were in power for a few short months. We were bearing the consequences of the ten or 12 years of neglect which we had behind us when the Liberals had been in power. As usual, a Tory government was following a Liberal government, and they were getting ready to say, "Tory times are hard times." Then the darned fools forgot themselves and they defeated us; the Liberal Party followed the Liberal Party and now we hear, "Liberal times are bad times." The people of Canada really know what causes bad times. It is the Liberal Party and Liberal policies that cause bad times. The Liberals are facing responsibility now for their own 12 years of neglect. So Liberal times are hard times, and the old slogan about Tory times being hard times are a result of the Tory party having to follow the Liberal Party in power every so often. But now the Liberals are in power and they are squirming and squealing. They are doing nothing. They are like a group of stuck pigs under a fence wondering how to get out from under it.
Let us hone in. What did the Liberal Party members say they were going to do when they were out of power? Here is what was said by the present Minister of DREE (Mr. Gray) before the commons committee on finance on October 30, 1979. He attacked the 14 per cent interest rate by saying:
-it will mean the loss of thousands of jobs; it will mean increases in the cost of living. It will probably bring the housing and construction industry to a halt-
It will put housing beyond the reach of most middle and lower-income Canadians. It will hurt small business-
-It will hurt farmers-and will add, therefore, to the cost of food.
That is what the minister said in October, 1979, when interest rates were 14 per cent. Today he is a member of the Government of Canada. Interest rates are far higher, but he does not think any longer about putting housing beyond the reach of most middle and low-income Canadians. He does not think any longer about bringing the housing industry to a halt. He does not care. He does not give a darn. He cares not a twit because he is in the warm embrace of the governmental bosom and could not care less for the next two or three years. He has cared less for the two years that have just passed. But that is what the minister said when he was in opposition.
What did the government's housing critic say when he was in opposition? He is now the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy). He is now the man responsible for the over one million unemployed that we have. He is just as sincere and dedicated now as he had been then. He was then the housing critic. On October 29, 1979, he said that if there is

February 24, 1982
Housing
a requirement to raise interest rates, there is an equal requirement to help those people who are hurt by those interest rate increases. That was the great Liberal principle when they were out of power. If interest rates have to rise, there is a requirement to help the people who are hurt by those interest rate increases. That was the great humanitarian Liberal principle of October, 1979. That minister, who has since become the hero of Canadian womanhood, announced what was the Liberal principle when the Liberals were in opposition.
What else did the Liberals say in those days? When it came to the election campaign, here is what the Prime Minister said about interest rates, as reported in the Toronto Star on February 10, 1980:
I would want to manage the economy in such a way that interest rales would in fact come down-because the economy would be administered in a sounder way.
That is something to laugh about, Mr. Speaker, that interest rates would come down because of the way this Prime Minister would manage the economy. The hypocrite has not attempted to manage the economy. When he did attempt to do so in the last month or two, it has been a disaster. Again, during the election campaign, as reported in The Toronto Sun for February 4, 1980, we read:
It is my belief we can manage the economy in a way that would allow us to have lower interest rates than we have now and I think we can have greater independence in interest rate policy.
If the Prime Minister thought that the economy could be administered in a sounder way than by bringing down interest rates, what has happened to him since? We know that he has visited practically every country in the world. But he has forgotten all about interest rates and how he was going to manage the economy and bring them down.
Here is what the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) said on October 25, 1979, in this chamber:
I deplore high interest rates. The minister has made the decision to impose high interest rates. I am not prepared to say at this point that it was the right decision.
That was the President of the Treasury Board. But now what is he prepared to say? He was not prepared at that point to say it was the right decision when interest rates were 14 per cent, but he has been there since when interest rates were 19 per cent and went up to 21.5 per cent. Now he is prepared to say that it was the right decision, now that he is in power himself. The President of the Treasury Board finds that it was the right decision. He does not mind 21 per cent and 22 per cent interest rates. He only deplores 14 per cent interest rates when there is someone else in the government. He does not deplore them when he himself is in the government and could do something about them. This chamber stinks. It is rife with the hypocrisy of the people who spoke like that when they were out of power. They have done nothing to follow up on what they said when they were out of power since they have been in power.
What was the Liberals' housing program in the last election? They are too shamefaced over there to even bawl, cackle or howl. They are quietly shamefaced as they listen to this recital of their treachery. The Liberals' housing policy for 1979-1980 was:
Our policy is guided by the basic principles of assisting low-income people to secure proper housing, and of increasing the affordability of ownership so more Canadians can choose between renting and owning.
That was the great principle the minister responsible for housing had when he was out of power. Now that he is in power, he does not give a darn about helping low-income people secure proper housing or increasing the affordability of ownership. All he has done is to bring this weak-kneed, spineless bill before the House on which he is now imposing closure to force it through. It is a pitiful rump of a bill that he has brought forward.
What else was said by this gentleman? I will not go too much further into this because it is too painful. In Toronto on January 12, 1980, the Prime Minister was giving his economic program to the people of Canada. He said:
This party will not simply stand by and let the recession come. We will fight it and overcome it.
That was the great Liberal principle on January 12, 1980. The Liberals would not stand by and let the recession come. They were going to fight it and overcome it. Has anybody seen a recession that has been fought and overcome lately? Has anyone seen a recession fought and overcome since the government got back in power in March, 1980? All I have seen is a bunch of pantywaist people falling on their faces in front of a recession, afraid to do anything. The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) brought in a budget that was the worst ever brought into this chamber that did exactly nothing to fight a recession but instead made it ten times worse.
What did the Liberals say after they got back into power? I will do this very quickly because I do not like inflicting this kind of punishment on the poor, dumb brutes opposite. Here is what they have said since they got back into power. The Minister of Finance said, as reported in the Montreal Gazette for March 19, 1980:
Mortgage interest relief for Canada's home owners depends in part on the oil deal Ottawa gets with Alberta, says federal Finance Minister Allan MacEachen.
He said mortgage interest relief depends on the deal Ottawa gets with Alberta. That was when he was just beginning his career as this sliven, a sliven to top all slivens in the portfolio of the Minister of Finance. In the fall of 1981 Canada got an oil deal with Alberta which is giving the minister billions and billions of additional revenue. Indirect taxation is up 54 per cent this year. Indirect taxes are up $8 billion. The Minister of Finance has got the money. Why does he not carry out that program of mortgage interest relief that he said depended upon the negotiations? He tried to blame Alberta about mortgage interest relief. Then the minister went to Halifax and on September 9, 1980, he said "it was to create jobs, improve living standards and promote greater equity that I took on the position of Minister of Finance." Never have more boastful words been uttered by a man who did less to carry them out. He took on the position to create jobs, improve living standards and promote greater equity. What a laugh. What a disappointment that the man does not resign his portfolio today. If he had any backbone, gumption or any streak of honesty at all in him, he would swallow those words, he would eat them right in front of us in this chamber the way he has failed after making those boastful remarks in Halifax, Nova
February 24, 1982

Scotia, on September 9, 1980. Then a few months later, on November 21, 1980, Canadian Press reported:
Canadians will have to accept a lower standard of living to adjust to higher energy prices. Finance Minister Allan MacEachen says.
Who said that? It was the Minister of Finance, the man who a few months before said that he would create jobs, improve living standards and promote greater equity. He said that in September, but in November he said that Canadians will have to accept a lower standard of living to adjust to higher energy prices. He said also:
We just can't as a country escape some adjustments in our standards of living for a time. That's a hard message but I think it just has to be put across.
If that is not hyprocrisy, if that is not the lowest of the low, if that is not twisting and turning because he could not see any way out, what is it? We have to get used to lower standards. We are not going to get used to more equity. We are not going to get used to more jobs. We are not going to get used to improved living standards for which he said he became Minister of Finance. But no, now his message is to get used to a lower living standard. That was never mentioned when the Liberals were seeking power.
Let us go on to the next month, Mr. Speaker, December 6, 1980. What did the Prime Minister say? The Prime Minister who told us what a wonderful job he was going to do on interest rates said that Canadians should change their spending priorities to maintain the same level of food on their tables while reducing spending in other areas. He said:
They don't have to accept less on their tables, but they might want to switch priorities and spend more on food than they are on other things.
That is the Prime Minister's theme in December 1980, after telling us how they were going to do such wonderful things for the Canadian people. Are they going to go to the electorate in the next election with the great slogan: Come, shorten your belt, tighten your belt, change your priorities, accept less on your tables, spend more on food than on other things? Is that the slogan for the next election? Are they going to promise Canadians dire straits in the next election? "Vote Liberal and we will make sure you are in dire straits." That should be their slogan in the next election.
On May 9, 1981, interest rates have gone berserk. The Ottawa Citizen says "Mortgages soar-we're on our own". This is what the Minister of Finance said:
It would be wrong for me to give advice to particular individuals as to how they are to manage their affairs.
He did not mind advising them what to do in the election. He said, "Vote Liberal and prices will come down". He gave them advice then, but now he is the powerful Minister of Finance of Canada, this sensitive man from Cape Breton, and
he says:
It would be wrong for me to give advice to particular individuals as to how they are to manage their affairs.
This Uriah Heep of all Uriah Heeps would not advise individual Canadians. He said the government would not bail
Housing
out individuals facing a mortgage renewal or first-time home buyers trapped by circumstances. The article says:
The minister noted that an analysis last year found most home owners could handle the payments resulting from higher rates.
This minister had the audacity to say that his analysis showed most home owners could handle the payments resulting from higher rates. Home owners of Canada out there looking on, the thousands of you, do you realize that you can handle these higher rates? Eighteen per cent, 19, 20, 21, 22? Don't be bothered by it; the Minister of Finance, Mr. MacEachen, says his analysis has found most of you can handle the payments resulting from higher rates. Can you hear that, Mrs. Judith Murphy down in my district of St. John's West? Don't worry, you are going to lose your home. Can you hear that, the 17 people whose homes are up for sale in my district? Just hear this: You are foolish, you should not have your house up for sale, you should not have allowed them to take your house from you. Why, you can handle the payments resulting from higher interest rates, according to that Minister of Finance of Canada, Mr. MacEachen.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. On a couple of occasions the hon. member has taken the liberty of referring to hon. members by their surnames. He should refer to them by the riding they represent.

I agree with you, Mr. Speaker. I can well understand why the Minister of Finance does not want anyone to know his name. If I were him, I would not want them to know my name either. So I agree with you completely.
Now I come to my final selection, of September 11, 1981. What have the great promises come to now? They are down in Ingonish pondering what they can do about interest rates, and the Prime Minister says he has no plans to offer general relief from record high mortgages and mounting energy prices. Any help will only be for those in, and I quote him, "absolute dire straits." That was not his economic program in 1979-80. You are only going to get help if you are in absolute dire straits. What is "absolute dire straits"? Well, one analogy I like to make is this. You are lying out there at the side of the road in winter, Mr. Speaker, without a stitch on. You do not have a home to go to or shed to crawl into. I would say that puts you in absolutely dire straits. What is this government's solution? If we look at the bill before us now, why, the minister responsible for housing and the Prime Minister are driving along in their big chauffeured Cadillac, or whatever it is, and they see this naked body at the side of the road. They stop. They are Liberals, they are very concerned when they see a naked figure at the side of the road in winter. They get out of the car, the Prime Minister takes the hands, the minister responsible for housing takes the feet and they move him off the road behind the trees so no one can see him. Now they have looked after your dire straits. That is the policy of this government, a policy which the people of Canada are not going to forget. They will never forget and never forgive you for leaving them in absolute dire straits, believe me.

Housing
What about the minister responsible for housing? A delegation of middle-class people in distress came here to Ottawa to see him. After getting the RCMP riot squad around him to make sure there would be no rough treatment, he met them and told them that something had to be done. These people are going to lose their homes and everything they have. He said, "Something has to be done and we will do something, I can tell you that." A positively Churchillian response to those people in their misery. After being in office for a year and a half, having defeated a government that was attempting to do something, he told them something has to be done and we will do something. The "something" he has done is in this pitiful piece of legislation before the House. What are they going to do? Well, there are 920,000 mortgage holders in the last half of 1981 and the first half of 1982 who had to renew their mortgages, most of them in trouble. The government is providing $38 million to help those 920,000 mortgage holders. Perhaps
12,000	will get some help. How do you get the help? If you are spending over 30 per cent of your income on mortgage payments, they will then give you assistance. If you have any equity in your home, they are going to give you another loan to add to the rest of your loans to meet higher interest payments. That is supposed to be help, and you have to pay it back some day. But if you have no equity left and you are paying over 30 per cent of your income on mortgage payments, then they are going to give you a grant of $3,000 to help meet the additional interest costs. That is the great program the minister referred to when he said something has to be done, and he will do something. He has done nothing, he has done less than nothing. He has shamed his government and his country, if this was all he could come up with.
Then there is the $112 million to help build 15,000 rental units. He has done nothing for tenants. There is no shelter allowance here. Mr. Speaker, when we presented our proposal to the House back in the fall of 1979 the Liberals and the NDP opposed it. They said, "This is no good, we want a shelter allowance to help the low-income home owner and tenant." Where is the shelter allowance? They have been there now for two years. They have increased taxes by many billions of dollars, 54 per cent in indirect taxes alone. A 31 per cent increase in revenues this year compared to last year. Where is the shelter allowance for tenants? There is nothing for tenants and home owners, nothing for anyone in this legislation on which the minister puts closure. He has the effrontery, the gall to come into this House and say we should rush through this pitiful piece of legislation. That is the best he can come up with for the people of Canada like my Mrs. Judith Murphy and the other people who are losing their homes down in Newfoundland this week under powers of sale. This is the best he can do for them. And the hypocritical Minister of Finance says to them that his surveys have shown that they can meet these higher costs, this doubling of interest rates. Disgusting hypocrisy, and the people of Canada are not going to forget it. They are not going to forget the members of the NDP who put them in the position where they could wreak this damage on the Canadian people, the same party which opposed the program we brought in to help the Canadian people. Well, what was that program? It was a program of mortgage interest
and property tax deductibility. It represented a major effort to help the Canadian people. It would have, in the year 1982, put $2,800 million in the pockets of home owners in Canada, whether they had a mortgage or not. Part of the program related to mortgage interest, and part to property taxes. That would have been the result had the legislation passed, had the NDP and Liberals not stopped us in their vicious desire to get back into power. Although they had been there for most of this century, they could not stand being out longer than seven months.
The government might have forgotten that. The government should have acted for the good of the people of this country and should not have stopped this legislation which would have provided $2.8 billion. Home owners paying $5,000 a year for mortgage interest would have received the maximum relief, amounting to $1,250, and would have received another $250 in relief from their property taxes. That was the maximum assistance they would have received under the program, implemented over four years. They would have received a quarter of the benefit in 1979, half of the benefit in 1980, three-quarters of the benefit in 1981, and the benefit of the full program this year, 1982. I believe $2,850 million was the total amount.
That was what we offered and what we wanted to put before the people of Canada. How would that help home owners with their mortgages? The average amount of assistance under our program to Canadian home-owning families this year would have amounted to $590 per family. I say to the ladies and gentlemen of Canada who are out there looking on that that would have helped them with their increased interest rates. That would have helped them to a considerable extent, and they would not have this kind of ruinous interest rate because the interest rates would have been considerably lower had we been left here unobstructed and had our policies gone into effect over the last two years, and had the tar sands gone ahead. We would not be hearing this anti-U.S. and antiprivate sector rhetoric. There would not be these vicious attacks on the Canadian dollar by the government, which leaves this government with nothing with which to defend the dollar but high, high, crucifying interest rates. No, the home owners of Canada would have had tremendous assistance had we been left there.
I will discuss further details of that program which was introduced in the House in December of 1979. It was to be phased in because we were fiscally responsible. It would have been phased in over four years with the full benefit in the 1982 tax year. It would have provided $2.8 billion. This year home owners would have received also another $1 billion from the energy tax credit, whether they paid income tax or not. You Canadians out there who are now looking on this chamber would have been receiving another $1 billion, amounting to a total of $3.8 billion to help you in your costs of meeting energy increases. Each family of four would have received $220. You would get the maximum if you had a maximum income of $25,000. It was a program to help lower-income people.

That was stopped by the Liberal Party. That was stopped by the hon. members of the New Democratic Party. That is the party whose leader goes across this country, the galloping Uriah Heep of Canadian politics, twisting his hands, telling people how badly off they are and how his heart bleeds for the Canadian people who are paying such high interest rates and paying so much on their houses, and paying so much on their mortgages, and paying so much to the banks. He rubs his hands and tells them how sympathetic he is concerning their situation when he is the one who put them in the position of dire straits. He is the one who put them back under the tutelage of the Liberal Party of Canada. That gentleman should also take a hint and resign, if he is worried about the people of Canada and what they are suffering from today. He is the one who is in bed with the government and its economic policies and in bed with the government and its constitutional policies. He could not wait to get into bed with all of those policies.
You were in bed with the oil companies.
Pardon?
You were in bed with the oil companies.
The only person with whom I go to bed-I will not mention her name in this chamber. 1 am not in bed with anyone, except occasionally.
Oh, oh!

Where does this lead us to? Here we have this piece of legislation, Bill C-89. The minister who puts his name to this piece of legislation will go down in Canadian history as-what is the name of the meanest character Charles Dickens ever invented?
John Crosbie!
Uriah Heep!

Uriah Heep, Fagin-he will go down as the most miserly housing minister in Canadian history. If the minister responsible for housing could not do better with the Minister of Finance than he did, he should resign. He should quote, to the Minister of Finance, some of these quotations that I found without any trouble at all. He should quote to the minister. Do hon. members know what the Minister of Finance said? He said his budget had three themes: restraint, equity and economic renewal. He should start to ask the Minister of Finance, "Where is the equity in your budget, minister? You are giving me $38 million to meet the needs of the 950,000 mortgage holders, or whatever the number may be, whose mortgages are coming due this year."
