Mr. Speaker, it is far from the first time that 1 have risen to debate this sort of bill in the House. Notable times which occur to me were in 1973, 1975, concerning two bills of this sort, and in 1979, to name a few that I can recall. The first time, in 1973, I had some advice for the government which essentially boiled down to two words, which were to "get out" of the housing field if it wanted to help matters for Canadian people.
That is what they are doing!

That is what the government has not done over the nine years since I first made those remarks. However, the minister of the day, the Hon. Ron Basford, did take my advice in that he got out. First of all, he got out of the housing and urban affairs ministry; a few years later, he got out of the justice ministry; and a few years ago, he got out of Parliament altogether and set himself up as a private citizen in Vancouver. Maybe at the time of the next election, whenever it comes, hon. members opposite will find that they are getting out of this House too, or at least out of this government, so that the enterprise sector of our country can start to provide some housing which is so badly needed by everyone in Canada.
However, did they get out? Did they do anything about trying to encourage the enterprise system? I refer the House to the public accounts of 1981, Volume III, the financial statements of Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation which indicates that the No. 1 liability of the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation is borrowings from the Government of Canada which amount to over $10 billion. It has borrowed $10,085 million from the Government of Canada.
We know where that money came from, do we not, Mr. Speaker? It came from the taxpayers of Canada who are out there struggling, trying to provide themselves with housing while this burden of taxation is around their necks. Not only has $10 billion been borrowed from the taxpayers of Canada and put into the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation for whatever purposes the minister may have had in mind, but there is also an item in the public accounts showing grants, contributions and subsidies on behalf of the minister for the year ending December 31, 1980, and the total charged to the minister, as per Schedule 5 in those public accounts, is $997 million. Three million short of $1 billion has been charged off in the current fiscal year to the minister for grants, contributions and subsidies. That is a trend which started in 1979 with $840 million, amounting, as I say, to $997 million in 1980. The current estimates cut that slightly, but it is still well around the $900 million mark for the current fiscal year for the minister's discretionary expenditures on housing.

February 24, 1982
Housing
I want to refer back to 1975 for a moment, which is seven years ago, after all. In the debate at that time, 1 quoted an excerpt from The Vancouver Province of September, 1974. The editorial in The Vancouver Province observed that:
'-our housing difficulties, particularly in the rental field, compose a classic case of problem creation by government.
It continued:
We did not begin to experience real rental shortages in this country until the federal government removed the tax incentives that channelled a lot of private money into rental accommodation.'
Do we remember what things were like prior to 1971 when this government changed accounting principles, changed the taxation principles, and drove out large segments of the enterprise sector from the housing field? All of a sudden, the government changed the rules for accounting and said, "Yes, if you manufacture something, or if you have a big industrial plant, you can deduct the capital cost allowance, the depreciation, from your plant and machinery and from your building". However, it also said, "If you are providing housing for Canadians who cannot afford to buy or build their own, if you are building rental housing in Canada, you will not be able to deduct a loss created by depreciation, by capital cost allowance, from other income".
Having completely destroyed or perverted the accounting principles that had been accepted in this country for a hundred years and more, the result was predictable. High income Canadians, those in the position to invest in housing, have to protect themselves and invest their funds somewhere. However, those whom we want to encourage to provide housing and invest in Canada were driven out of the housing business. That is when the shortages started.
I have often said here and in other places that we have no housing shortage in Canada. The minister should know that; he need only count up the unsold, speculatively built units that are found across this country. There is no housing shortage in Canada. What we have is a money shortage among certain people who cannot find housing they can afford. This is the affordable housing that we on this side of the House talk about. We talk about it all the time. The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell) talks about affordable housing. This is the problem.
If you have enough money, you can go anywhere in Canada, even in Point Grey, as the member for Vancouver East says, or in my riding of Vancouver Quadra, and buy a single family lot for $500,000 cash, if you have it. Then you can build a house. Or you can do what others are doing in Vancouver and buy a run down house for $245,000, tear it down and build a new one.
There is no housing shortage in this country. What we have is a money shortage. This government has taken the money, splattered it all over the map and has not hit the target of where the money is needed.
The hon. member for Vancouver East sometimes thinks my housing policies are strange. However, I find support for my policies from unexpected sources. The Canadian Organization
of Public Housing Tenants may seem a strange outfit for me to call on for support. It turns out they realize the same problems that I have seen and which this government has presented to them. They wrote the following in their official newsletter, "The Raised Roof'. I quote from a 1979 speech that I made in this House. I find I am the greatest quoter of my own speeches in this House. The first page of this "Raised Roof' newsletter is headlined "The problem is not really housing". In their lead editorial they say, and I quote:
The group has tried to show members of government, housing corporations and authorities that the problem in housing is not really housing, but the entire economic question, of which housing is merely one part.
That is what I have been saying for a long time. I have heard others on this side of the House say the same, but the government cannot see that there are individuals with problems. They seem to think there is a housing problem. What do we have now in Canada? We have a great underutilized private sector that wants to provide housing, but they are unable to do that because of the whole economic climate that the minister's colleagues have imposed upon us.
These remarks that I am referring to were made seven years ago, but nothing has improved. I will not say nothing has changed, but nothing has improved. We might ask ourselves what went wrong.
I mentioned 1971 when the government changed the basic accounting policies and said that losses created by capital cost allowance depreciation could no longer be deducted. I compared that with the fact that one can deduct capital cost allowance depreciation on machinery or a factory building. It is absolute nonsense when you compare the merits of the two cases.
What happened? Why did we get into this terrible situation in which we now find ourselves? Why has it become so much worse over the past three, seven or ten years? We saw that high-income individuals had stopped investing in rental housing because the climate had been made so bad for them. It started off with the policies of this government. This government tends to produce ministers of finance who have strange attitudes when it comes to economic policies that create problems for all Canadians.
The minister of finance seven years ago was one named John Turner. He was the first to sound the idea of taxing the imputed value of home ownership to see whether the government could raise more money. After all, those who owned their own homes and had equity in their homes, whether it was clear title or just an equity, did not pay any taxes on that income. I do not know whether it was that idea or one of his other ideas that caused him to get out of the finance portfolio. In any event, he is gone.
There has been a succession of others who have not really done anything other than to pay lip service to the economic problems we have in Canada today. Talk about strange things. We now have a Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) who wants to tax income before it is received. I am referring to the life insurance situation. He not only wants to tax income
February 24, 1982

before it is received, but tax income that may never be received. On deferred income securities, the Minister of Finance wants to accrue income for tax purposes.
The minister has made a broadside attack in his current budget on the institution of marriage by denying married people the same tax benefits as two single people who live together are entitled to. I refer here to the exemption of capital gains tax on a second residence. The married couple will be denied that even though two single people will be entitled to it. If a widow and a widower should happen to get together and want to marry, this government will impose a terrible penally on them. The pension benefits of the widow and widower would be taken away from both of them whereas they would continue if they stayed single.
The Minister of Finance says that a businessman can deduct the wages of those who help him earn his income, such as a secretary, stock clerk or shop clerk, but a working mother who must have an attendant or some other child care expense can only deduct $1,000 for tax purposes, even though she may have a nanny living in the house whom she pays $7,000 for that service. If she takes advantage of a child care service, even the one that will be offered by the House of Commons this year, it will cost about $4,000. The Minister of Finance says, however, that only $1,000 can be deducted.
The Minister of Finance is supposed to be encouraging people to work in Canada and to pay taxes. These women are working because they want to or need to, or both, yet they are being denied the proper deductions to which they should be entitled.
The Minister of Finance says that interest expenses on certain investments in Canadian businesses will not be deductible, another departure from generally accepted accounting principles. It has always been accepted that if money, particularly interest, was laid out for the purpose of earning income, even if not this year's income, it would be a deductible expense.
Many Canadians invest in Canadian businesses, not with the prospect of immediate profit. They may be willing to wait one, two, three or five years. Sometimes they do not know. The Minister of Finance, who is creating this bad economic climate for the housing industry, is also creating this bad economic climate for all Canadians who want to invest in Canada.
It is not only the federal government that is creating these problems and has created the problems in the housing field. The provincial governments have also got into the act. Rent controls have been in existence in a number of provinces. These have prevented economic rents being charged and new buildings were therefore not built. Housing was not provided where it was needed.
New buildings were exempted from rent controls after a few years because provincial governments realized that there was no new construction. They indicated that if new buildings were rented they would relax the rent controls. Of course, the predictable happened although those governments did not see it. Older buildings which were still under rent control became
Housing
uneconomic units. They were torn down and replaced with new, more expensive housing which just created more problems for those people this minister responsible for housing is trying to help through this feeble bill which is before us today.
It is no wonder that there was not a flood of new units once the others were freed from rent controls. Investors were nervous about entering the market with brand-new, expensive units while many units were already on the market under rent control, resulting in severe competition to the newly-built units.
What else has the federal government tried to do during the last decade? We have had an alphabet soup of programs and one which comes to mind now is ARP, the assisted rental program. This was a scheme whereby a monthly subsidy was paid to developers to provide new units at a rent less than the economic rent. It did not have anything to do with the tenants. All that tenants knew was that they were getting a good deal on their rent. This scheme depended entirely on continuing high inflation for its success. Not one minister responsible for housing who would dream up an assisted rental program such as this could have expected it to work unless he had the collaboration-and even the collusion-of the Minister of Finance, who would guarantee that inflation would continue at a good high rate. If that were not the case the building owner would ultimately go bankrupt because his debt was ever mounting and his interest liability would eventually begin.
Did all this government intervention help? Did it result in more housing units? Apparently not enough, according to the minister. My colleague from St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) has quoted some figures on the shortfall of current housing starts to meet the needs of Canadians.
What did the government then decide to do? It gave us more alphabet soup. It introduced MURBs, a program designed to encourage multiple unit residential buildings. That program was introduced around 1976. It was only a restoration of the principles which were in effect in 1971. But did the program admit that it was wrong in cutting off this very valuable and efficient source of housing in 1971? No; it brought in a new portion of the alphabet which it called MURBs. It would not want to admit that it was wrong by restoring the old policy.
I suppose the MURB program was designed to confuse the industry and it certainly did that, along with the rest of Canadians. The plan was then to have the program expire at a specified date. The industry did not know when this date would be or whether it would expire at all. The industry put pressure on the government, which responded that it might be continued or it might not be. The industry did not know what to do.
This illustrates how the enterprise system has demonstrated time and again that it can tolerate any set of rules which the government may wish to impose upon it but cannot tolerate unknown rules and sudden changes to the rules. This uncertainty upsets all industrial planning. The government has not realized that fact yet.

February 24, 1982
Housing
As a result of this uncertainty, the housing industry was upset. It was continually turned off, then turned on, to the point that it did not know whether it was coming or going. The industry hoped that the MURB program would be renewed, which it was on numerous occasions, but always at the last moment. Finally, last December the MURB program was allowed to die. Whether it is a final death, only time will tell. Perhaps the housing minister will be able to resurrect it, but 1 am sure he will not get help from the Minister of Finance.
What was the result of the MURB program being finished in December? It created a panic in the housing industry which in its plans for 1982 it had laid on all this land, and which would not qualify for a MURB if it did not dig the foundations and instal the footings by the end of December. The predictable result of that was that jobs had to be done at overtime rates with high rentals on equipment which eventually resulted in added costs to construction. This will result in higher rents for those who occupy those MURBs.
I have talked enough about the government's programs. I would like to talk now about interest rates. Do interest rates not have something to do with the housing industry? If they do, the minister does not seem to confer with the Minister of Finance in order to do anything about it. The House will recall that one of the first acts of the Clark government in 1979 was to refer the problem of interest rates which were already too high at that time to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. I had the honour to be the chairman of that standing committee during the Thirty-first Parliament. It was a serious study which was conducted by members of the House. Economists, those knowledgeable about interest rates, consultants and professors were summoned from all across the country to try to advise the Standing Committee on Finance. Trade and Economic Affairs on how to resolve the problems created by high interest rates and show what avenues were open to the government at the time.
It is curious that the finance critic for the Liberal Party at that time who was a member of that committee, the hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray), who is the present Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, referring in his remarks to the hon. member for St. John's West who was then minister of finance, said to the Commons finance committee on October 30, 1979, that:
Your high interest rate policy would slow down the economy: it will mean the loss of thousands of jobs; it will mean increases in the cost of living. It will probably bring the housing and construction industry to a halt, with thousands of jobs being lost in those sectors.
It will put housing beyond the reach of most middle and lower-income Canadians. It will hurt small business, which depends on bank borrowing to operate. It will hurt farmers, who have the same dependency on bank borrowing and will add, therefore, to the cost of food.
That remark was attributed to the member for Windsor West in the Commons finance committee, October 30, 1979.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, an election ensued not too many months after that statement. During that election campaign and afterwards, that same member who is now the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Regional
Economic Expansion promised the House, his electors and the people of Canada that if interest rates did not stay down or could not be brought down he would resign. I will give a comparison between what the interest rates were and what they are now.
Before I do that, I would like to recall some remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who, during the election campaign in Toronto, on February 10, 1980, promised that he would manage the economy in such a way that interest rates would, in fact, come down because the economy would be administered in a sounder way. The government may be trying to administer the economy in some way but it certainly is not in a sounder way. If I were in the Liberal government and administering the economy with the result it has achieved, I would not want to admit it.
Where were the interest rates then and what are they now? The interest rates which were causing the hon. member for Windsor West such panic at that time, in the 1980 election, were as follows: the Bank of Canada rate was 14 per cent, the average mortgage rate was 13.5 per cent and the chartered bank prime rate was 15 per cent. By August, 1981, the bank rate had climbed to a record 21.24 per cent; the chartered bank prime rate was 22.75 per cent. Some lenders were charging in excess of 22 per cent for first mortgages.
The government opposite has had a bit of luck since then-I do not think it could be attributed to good planning or to anything but good luck-and mortgage rates are currently closer to 19 per cent than the 22 per cent rate. However, that is a far cry from the mortgage rate of 15 per cent about which the Liberal opposition was complaining.
We know what this government has done. An hon. member who is now a minister threatened to resign. The government has done nothing about interest rates or, at least, nothing which has had any effect.
During the Thirty-first Parliament our government put forward a proposal which was, I think, one day away from passage, the so-called mortgage interest and property tax deductibility scheme. Some members of the Liberal opposition were ready to stand up for it. Some had voted for it at earlier stages. That bill was debated for about seven days when finally the axe fell on it. This bill has been debated four and a half days, and the minister stood up today and told us that that is enough. He told us he has to get this puny bill through in a hurry. I will talk about the bill more in a moment. The minister is giving us notice that tomorrow the provisions of Standing Order 75C will come into play, and we will have a debate about that.
The mortgage interest and tax deductibility scheme we introduced in the Thirty-first Parliament would have helped every one of those Canadians who are having trouble now because of the economic policies of this government. Even prior to the introduction of our bill anyone with some money and some good tax advice could have arranged his affairs to
February 24, 1982

have his interest made deductible in any event. The bill we introduced was simply an attempt to bring all Canadians onto an equitable footing so that all Canadians could deduct interest-and property taxes too-paid on their principal residences.
Because of the inaction of this government with respect to that particular scheme, the situation which has developed is ludicrous. With the markets we have people are forced to take back second mortgages on the sale of their homes, and the interest on those mortgages taken back is treated as income for tax purposes. This is a regime enforced by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Rompkey). At the same time, when an individual goes and buys another home-just a replacement home, nothing special or different-and has to borrow because he does not have all his money out of his former home, he is not allowed, under the rules of this government, to deduct the interest on the new mortgage in calculating his taxable income. The government has imposed a double jeopardy on people like this who want to change homes for whatever reason. These moves might be required because of jobs, family reasons or whatever.
What we might question at this point is what this bill is all about. Bill C-89, which has been before us for these few days and on which the government opposite is imposing closure, will provide an "opportunity" for Canadians to go deeper into debt. Is that not a great favour from the government? It is encouraging Canadians to go deeper into debt. I have always felt that government should encourage people to become selfsufficient and retire their debts. But no, this plan allows individuals who are faced with higher mortgage payments to borrow more money and to go deeper into debt. Of course, the government will provide insurance so that lenders will not be jeopardized; they will be assured of getting their money back.
This bill also proposes to provide legislative authority for interest-free loans of up to $7,500 per unit to landlords constructing new buildings, as outlined in the budget. Seventy-five hundred dollars a unit might be all right in some cities such as Ottawa; perhaps the land cost per rental unit in Ottawa might be $10,000 up to $20,000. But in cities like Calgary and Vancouver $7,500 per unit would be absolutely worthless. Land costs in those areas are such that this bill would not encourage the construction of a single unit. Even if landlords get $7,500 loans, they will have to repay the loans, and rents will have to reflect the amortization of those loans from the government.
There are a couple of other things this bill proposes which are more serious and prehaps even more dangerous. The rate of interest payable on loans issued by the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation would be determined by the corporation and not by the governor in council. This Parliament is supposed to make decisions dealing with taxpayers' money. As I said earlier, $10 billion is a lot of taxpayers' money for the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation to be dealing with. The government likes to take responsibility for taking decisions away from Parliament and making such decisions through the governor in council. I do not think we should forget that there were some 3,500 orders in council in the last
Housing
fiscal year. However, this responsibility is being taken away not only from Parliament but also from the governor in council-the cabinet-and it is being given to the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation. That is a very serious transfer of power away from elected representatives. I hope the minister is paying attention to this because he is losing control as much as all other Members of Parliament.
Another aspect of this bill is an observance of the fact that as many as 40,000 Canadian families may lose their homes because of the current high interest rates. A family income of $45,000 is now needed to afford an average-priced home in Canada. Hon. members do not need to be reminded of the mail they received from their constituents with respect to the current salary for a Member of Parliament of $48,000, which is only $3,000 more than the basic $45,000 needed to afford an average home in Canada. The salary of a Member of Parliament is not considered to be an average salary, it is considered to be a high salary, so where does that leave the average Canadian who earns less than $45,000 when he wants to buy a home?
Serious shortages are developing in many centres, and the number of housing starts in the last half of 1981 was barely half the number needed to keep pace with housing requirements.
I think I have said enough for this kind of bill. In closing, I just want to say that for over ten years the housing issue has been tossed around by this government. I referred earlier to the Hon. Ron Basford, who had this responsibility when he was minister of state for urban affairs. Not only has that minister come and gone but the ministry of state for urban affairs has also come and gone. I cannot remember who had responsibilty for housing in the meantime, but now the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove) is responsible for housing in this country, and I can only remark that this indicates the lack of importance this government attaches to the housing issue. Housing is a very important Field, but it is a responsibility of the minister responsible for public works, a subject which is also very important.
We on this side of the House say that this bill is totally inadequate and misguided. The government should give the enterprisers of this country who are just waiting to get out there and build houses the opportunity to provide the housing Canadians need. They would provide it at rates which are suitable to the market, and they would sell their housing. This government should concern itself with making sure that there is no shortage of money for those who need affordable housing and making sure there is no shortage of policies which would provide economic soundness to this country.

February 24, 1982
Housing

Madam Speaker, the hon. member mentioned that the salary of a Member of Parliament is $48,000, I do not want him to mislead people. Anyone who works 15 or 16 hours a day, seven days a week, can make that salary anywhere else in Canada.

Madam Speaker, I rise to take part in the debate on Bill C-89 which proposes certain amendments to the National Housing Act, recognizing that it is one of the most important pieces of legislation to come before Parliament for some time.
There is a very serious housing crisis in Canada today. As Members of Parliament we had a right to expect that the government would come forward with serious and responsible solutions to that crisis, but I regret to say that Bill C-89 fails completely to address the concerns of my constituents in the municipality of Burnaby and of Canadians generally. I say that not only from the perspective of the provision of rental housing and ensuring that Canadians have sufficient funds to be able to afford adequate housing, but as the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke) indicated, also from the perspective of employment and jobs. 1 mean the jobs that thousands and thousands of Canadians could be filling if the government would only respond to the crisis that faces the people of Canada.
Some people may ask on what basis 1 identify the situation as a crisis. Mr. Speaker, in the last several months I have listened very carefully to the people of Burnaby. In response to a questionnaire which I circulated with a newsletter, 700 constituents have told me how they are affected by the housing policies of the Liberal government. I have also received many letters from constituents outlining their concerns about the housing situation in Burnaby and in British Columbia generally. I have received phone calls and many people have come to my constituency office to explain-not in alarmist tones but often in tones of sadness, despair and with a lack of hope for the future-how they are affected by the housing crisis.
In some instances several generations are involved-the children of my constituents, the young people faced with the tragedy of knowing that there is virtually no possibility of obtaining their own home in their lifetime under the policies of the present government, their parents, senior citizens who are in very serious difficulty. There are long waiting lists for affordable accommodation for senior citizens. This is a very serious concern that the government has failed to address.
Finally, I heard from my constituents at a large housing rally held in a school in my constituency in November last year. At that time men and women, young and old, came from all parts of Burnaby to express their concern and anger about the failure of the government to act on what must surely be recognized as a fundamental social right in a democratic and civilized society-the right to warm, clean and affordable housing.
As I said, my constituents are concerned and they are angry. I am here today to take part in the debate on Bill C-89 in
order to express, on their behalf, their demand that the government take responsible, tough and effective action now-not in the future-to deal with the housing crisis in Canada.
I mentioned the questionnaire which I circulated in my constituency. I do not want to take the time of the House to read all the responses, but I think the minister and the House should hear how my constituents and their families are affected by the government's failure to respond to the housing crisis. A renter in Burnaby replied:
We, a family of 4, have had to move several times to be able to afford the place we live. Still where we live now we are having a very hard time, but we cannot find a cheaper place.
At this rate we will never own our own home and if rents go any higher we won't be able to rent-
A Burnaby home owner who lives on Ewart Street in South Burnaby wrote:
Our payments have jumped from $511.00 to $818.00 per month, almost half our income per month.
They added that extras or home improvements are out of the question for them. Their interest rate went from 10.75 per cent to 21 per cent. Another Burnaby home owner replied:
Both husband and wife must work to maintain home, plus we rent part of our house to a couple to help cover the mortgage, and help the other couple too-
Having a family is out of the question, Mr. Speaker. What kind of sociological impact will the policies of this government have upon Canadian society today? Another Burnaby renter writes:
The chances of my owning a home seem remote. I don't feel the government should deny me this opportunity with their present policies-
Another Burnaby renter from Forest Grove Drive replied:
Can't afford a house as rent etc. has gone up so much in B.C. We have filed for bankruptcy-
A resident of Saturna Drive wrote:
Yes, as a young professional it is impossible for me to expect to be a home owner, given the mortgage rates, despite a reasonably good income-
A home owner on Portland Street in south Burnaby wrote:
Because of the "don't care'' attitude of big business and big government, we will be forced to cut back our retirement dreams in order to pay the bank to keep our homes, while bank profits soar-
These are just a representative example of the hardship being faced by my constituents in Burnaby, Mr. Speaker. Another renter writes:
My rent is roughly 60 per cent of my total income which means I must cut basic and pleasure spending-
The writer adds that his diet has been affected by the housing policies of the government.
That is the devastating effect that the lack of a comprehensive and humane housing policy is having on my constituents in Burnaby. Not only are interest rates unacceptably high, but it is virtually impossible for people to find a home at an affordable price.
I have a few clippings from recent issues of The Vancouver Sun and The Vancouver Province. What is commonly known as a "handyman special" is advertised for $125,000. The advertisement says that if you can overlook some traffic and do

a bit of upgrading-and there is not much of a view, apparently-you can get a house for $125,000 in Burnaby. Another advertisement triumphantly claims that the price is reduced by $20,000 to only $259,000 for a basic three-bedroom bungalow in South Burnaby. Another is listed as "builder's own" for $189,000.

The government is condemning thousands and thousands of Canadians in my constituency of Burnaby to totally inadequate levels of accommodation, Mr. Speaker.
The government says, "Let us get on with Bill C-89". The fact of the matter is that if the government was serious and brought forward legislation which dealt in a responsible manner with the housing crisis, we would be the First to support it. Bill C-89 is totally inadequate to deal with the real concerns of Canadians in the housing field.
It is the Liberal scheme of caring and sharing.

As the hon. member for Beaches (Mr. Young) puts it, it is the Liberal scheme of caring and sharing.
My constituents are angry and concerned about the government's failure to address what is unquestionably a housing crisis for all British Columbians; they feel a lack of hope for the future.

Our housing policy can be summarized in three words: Pierre Elliott Trudeau.

This telegram is reflective of many other people in British Columbia who quite rightly rejected Conservative policies on housing in Canada. The Conservatives took steps to totally dismantle CMHC.
Hurray!

-and turned over to his friends in the private sector. In a moment I will deal with the friends of

How much?
The hon. member for Vancouver Quadra asks how much.

A pittance.

I guess they are happier with the policies of the Conservative Party, and again that is not surprising.
What we must recognize is that both the Liberal Party and the Conservative Party are squarely in the pockets of the land developers and speculators in Canada today. It is no wonder that they are so bankrupt when it comes to policies to benefit home owners, renters and workers at this time of housing crisis. It is no wonder they want to remove rent controls in Canada; they have to pay back their friends in the land development community. They are just looking after their friends.
What about our mortgage interest deductibility proposal?

We in the NDP have a different approach to housing in Canada. It is a fundamentally different approach. We say that every Canadian is entitled to clean, warm, affordable housing as a fundamental right, just as they are entitled to health care, to proper education, to adequate diet and to a clean and wholesome environment. In fact, we feel so strongly about this that we proposed an amendment to the Charter of Rights and Freedoms that would recognize these as fundamental rights. Because as Frank Scott put it so eloquently, "the trappings of democracy hang loosely on an emaciated body politic". We need all of them. We need those fundamental rights to proper housing and the other rights that I suggest.
We have a positive alternative for housing. I am quite prepared to put it on the record today. We suggest that interest rates must be lowered, and lowered quickly.

The hon. member opposite asks by how much. 1 welcome his contribution to this debate-and his suggestions as to how far we should be lowering interest rates. What we have said is that interest rates should be lowered to one point above the rate of inflation today. That would have an immediate and dramatic impact on the housing crisis in Canada.
We suggest that banks should set aside a specific proportion of their lending portfolios for long-term mortgages at lower rates, primarily for first-time buyers. It is about time this government came to its senses and recognized that the thousands of construction workers and forestry workers looking for jobs to meet a real need for affordable housing in Canada should be put back to work. Some say "Well, you are not in government." I point to the government of Manitoba which has recently announced a major program along the lines I have suggested today that will be of significant help to the renters and home owners in the province of Manitoba.
What about another large group in my constituency, the students? There is a serious problem with student housing, particularly in my constituency of Burnaby in which is located Simon Fraser University, the B.C. Institute of Technology, which is the province's only high-technology training institute, and the Pacific Vocational Institute. BCIT graduates some 1,900 students annually.
Order, please.

2,000	students require housing at BCIT. Many of them who cannot find housing are from rural parts of British Columbia and are denied an adequate education in these very important

high technology areas. The demand has been increasing over past years. In fact, it would need 6,000 students to meet the demand for graduates from BCIT. Students at BCIT, PVI and SFU had to persuade the politicians that it would be disruptive to toss out students from these illegal suites. That is the situation we are in. Finally, Simon Fraser University, also located in my constituency, shares many of the same problems. Simon Fraser University has a critical situation on its hands. There are over
9,000	students at SFU. On-campus housing is adequate for only a small fraction of those students. There are 210 apartments on campus and a 225-bed dormitory. In September, 1981, 3,200 applicants applied for on-campus housing. There were 300 applicants for 20 beds. Where do the rest of those students go? They either go into substandard housing, basement suites where they are doubling and tripling up, or they are giving up and returning to their communities in despair and being denied the education to which they are so properly entitled.

I have a few more remarks on elements of this legislation that I believe should be changed. There are some serious problems with the provisions respecting mortgage financing. In many instances, Bill C-89 will do nothing but ensure a number of mortgage gimmicks, gimmicks that do not benefit the borrower in the end but which will certainly benefit the wealthy lenders, the banks, friends of the Liberal and Conservative parties.

Even the bankers recognize the folly of this government program. I quote Peter Carter, who was then assistant general manager for retail lending and mortgage services with the Royal Bank of Canada:
As a responsible banker, working in a consumer-oriented society, I just cannot agree with a plan that sees the borrower ending up after five years owing more money than he borrowed in the first place.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the Liberal government's answer. That is Liberal economic policy. That is the Liberal government's answer to the housing crisis and we reject it.

I suppose it is a bit convoluted to my own way of seeing things, but their rationale seems to be self-evident. They preferred to face defeat rather than deal with the housing bill.

"Pass that measure as rapidly as you can because we need that in the housing industry". These fellows are sitting
on their hands over there. Look at them! They are all sitting on their hands-
I want to speak.

-waiting for something to happen because, of course, they do not want to present any initiatives of their own. In effect, I feel that housing needs a shot in the arm.

Everybody is agreed on that. As far as housing is concerned, well, I come from northern Ontario, and in my area, there have been substantial lay-offs in the forestry industry because there is very little demand for construction lumber, which has led to production cuts and the lay-offs in question. The House will recall that not long ago, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) announced that a federal-provincial agreement had been concluded with the province of Ontario under which his department will be promoting jobs in the forestry industry in northern Ontario for 2,000 workers who were laid off because of a lack of markets. Obviously, since those markets include more than just the Canadian market, this bill or any other bill, for that matter, will not be able to generate a recovery in the housing market that would increase employment in my area, because the majority of forestry products from my area are exported to the United States, and when their market is slack, this obviously reduces the number of jobs in my part of the country. Mr. Speaker, it is a recognized fact that the main cause of these lay-offs is high interest rates, which in turn are affected by high inflation rates, because if we analyse the situation, the main problem, and everyone will agree, is the high rate of inflation which has been going on for far too long. The government has approached this question by saying that it will bring down inflation. Thus, interest rates will drop and lower interest rates will increase our economic stability, which means that people will be prepared to invest in business and housing. Once those investments have been made, the demand for housing and for lumber used in housing construction will increase and create jobs in my part of the country. Meanwhile, I am most indebted to the Minister of Employment and Immigration who chose my area for the purpose of assisting those people in the north who have lost their jobs because of the labour market situation.
In effect, the agreement that will allow approximately 2,000 temporarily laid-off lumber and forestry workers to continue working in forestry-related activities during the current downturn in the industry was a very good initiative on the part of the Minister of Employment and Immigration. It required not only his will and that of the government, but the will of the province of Ontario which provided co-operation, as well as the

forest products manufacturers in northern Ontario who recognized that there is now a soft market in the lumber industry.
I am very confident that there is a building demand in the marketplace for housing. There is an increase, not a dramatic but a gradual increase, in the number of family formations. There is a relatively low vacancy rate in most rental markets in Canada. Therefore, there is a demand, but that demand will not be satisfied when interest rates are volatile. It will be satisfied once interest rates are brought down as a result of inflation being brought down and the whole is stabilized. That is the basic aim of the government's policy.
I am very pleased at the initiatives being taken by the minister responsible for housing. However, I am somewhat dismayed at the lack of understanding, comprehension and especially foresight demonstrated by members of the opposition when they speak very briefly in response. I suggest they have no knowledge at all of the real world as it relates to Bill C-89 or to the current economic climate. Let me say that this government is determined to demonstrate leadership and restraint and to recognize the principle of equity in putting new programs in place. I applaud these measures that have been proposed by the minister of housing.
Now, for the sake of clarification and edification of members opposite so that they may more fully understand what these amendments to the National Housing Act will accomplish, let me review some of the proposals briefly.
First, the amendments would allow Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation to have a greater impact on the supply of rental accommodation. That is most important. For many years now there have been certain business restrictions regarding the operation of CMHC in the marketplace. These amendments will enable CMHC effectively to resolve these difficulties.
For example, in the recent past premiums charged for graduated payment mortgages were inadequate regarding the business risks involved, and the deteriorating markets over the past four years have not helped the situation. It is to such an extent that premiums even on ordinary NHA home owner loans have been marginally inadequate to cover the risk.
The solution to this problem is before us. The amended legislation would allow CMHC to adjust mortgage insurance premiums and to set them at a level that would be appropriate for the risk involved. It would also allow CMHC the wherewithal to cover the cost and expenses of doing business. In short, CMHC would have the same flexibility with regard to premiums as a private insurer.
The advantages would be obvious, even to the most clouded thinker, and Lord knows there are a lot of clouds on the other side and very little in terms of silver lining.

Clouded stinkers?

I said clouded thinker. "Clouded stinker" would be unparliamentary.
Turn around.
As far as I am concerned, I am showing my best side to those who feel most comfortable with it.
Show a little respect.

I am showing that as well.
Let me raise another important element in the legislation which the opposition has fogged in this debate, the Canada mortgage renewal plan. Between clouds and fog, we are getting the colour of the other side. Allegations have been made that the renewal plan is, in effect, too little and too late. To refresh the memories of members opposite, let us define who needs help the most.
It has been standard operating principle, followed not only by the government but by most major lending institutions in the country, that people should have a gross debt service ratio of not more than 30 per cent. That has been the rule of thumb. I recall that from when 1 was practising law. We talked of 27 per cent to 30 per cent being the gross debt service ratio. This means that Canadians who need help are those families and individuals who have to pay more than 30 per cent of their gross income on payments of principal, interest and taxes, and 50 per cent of condominium charges.
Think about it. This has been the benchmark that has been the guideline for years. Yet if you followed the convoluted rationale of some members opposite, we would be opening up the vault, no matter what the cost, to people who are not experiencing hardship and who can afford to make their payments without help from the government.
We can follow the rationale of the official opposition, the members of the Conservative Party, quite readily. They are the ones who advocated the mortgage interest tax deductibility program which, in effect, did not target any sector of the economy and favoured those with the most.
They would have loved it in North Bay.

The high flyers borrow a lot of money to buy a $200,000 house. They may pay $120,000 a year on a mortgage at today's 20 per cent interest rates and deduct the whole works from their income. Imagine that! What about the renter? He would have been left holding the bag, the one who would have had to make up the difference.
We believe that the amount available should be targeted to those most in need. Were it not for the frustration that we face from the members on the other side as a result of what they are doing to this bill, we would have had this in place a long time ago.
